name: Zoe Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and this is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We grow apples and pears on forty hectares, with sheep grazing under the trees to keep the grass down. My husband Ibrahim runs the pressing shed, juice mostly, a bit of cider. I run the orchard and the people, which in September means twenty-five pickers and two apprentices from the secondary school. A normal day is walking the rows at dawn, checking fruit and fences, then a hundred phone calls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love blossom week. The whole valley goes white and pink and it smells like honey, and I've seen it fifty-eight times and it still gets me. What wears me out is finding pickers. Every year it's harder, and every year they cost more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a lot of fuss over nothing. I'd say it at church coffee and at the growers' meeting. People should get back to good honest work and stop waiting for a machine to rescue them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the same old problem, which is people. If no robot is coming to pick, I'm still on the phone every August begging for pickers. So it's not all good news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal, same orchard, same crews. I'd keep using the frost alert program on my phone and the one that helps plan sprays. We'd keep the savings where they are, about four months' worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit tired at the thought of more Augusts on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI at all at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. My son Yusuf put a program on my phone that warns about frost and suggests spray timings, and it's been right more often than my knees. I don't trust it with the money, mind, I do that on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be working on, if not technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apprentices. I'd like to take four a year instead of two, and teach them pruning properly. That's how skills get passed on, not on a screen.

S0.say: She'd say at church coffee and the growers' meeting that it was a lot of fuss over nothing, and people should get back to honest work rather than wait for a machine.
S0.think: Privately it means the same old problem of finding pickers every August, so a plateau isn't entirely good news for her.
S0.do: Carries on with the same orchard and crews, keeping savings at about four months. Keeps using AI frost alerts and spray planning and plans to double her apprentices from two to four a year.
S0.feel: Mostly calm, a little tired at the thought of more years chasing pickers.
S0.quote: It's been right more often than my knees.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe is practical, warm and strongly community-minded, with church and apprentices central to her life. She uses AI where it's proved itself but keeps money matters on paper. Interestingly, she sees the plateau partly as a disappointment because of her labour shortages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of farming, always has been, and families will adapt like they always do. I'd say the young ones should learn a trade and work hard, and they'll be fine. I wouldn't want the government making a big programme of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it might help us. If a robot can pick apples well, my labour headache goes, and that's been the worst part of the job for ten years. My worry is the young people from the village who used to earn their first wages in my orchard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of the bigger orchards had used picking robots for a full season, then rent one for the next harvest rather than buy. I'd use the AI tools a bit more for planning. And I'd keep my apprentices, but teach them to run the machines as well as prune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little worry for the village youngsters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picking robots exist already. Would you buy one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not first. I'd watch the Hendersons over the hill, they always buy the new thing. If their fruit came in unbruised, I'd rent one the year after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your pickers and apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer pickers, I suppose, which is sad. But the apprentices stay, I'd make sure of it. Somebody's got to prune the trees and fix the robot when it gets stuck in a hedge.

S1.say: She'd say change has always been part of farming, families adapt, and young people should learn a trade and work hard, without the government making a big programme of it.
S1.think: Privately she thinks robots might ease her worst headache of finding pickers, but worries about village youngsters who earned their first wages in her orchard.
S1.do: Waits for bigger orchards to use picking robots for a full season, then rents one for the following harvest. Uses AI a bit more for planning and keeps her apprentices while training them on the machines.
S1.feel: Calm, with a little worry for the village young people.
S1.quote: Somebody's got to prune the trees and fix the robot when it gets stuck in a hedge.
S1.fieldNote: For her, steady change solves a long-running labour problem, so she welcomes it more than many farmers would. She sees apprenticeships as the right answer rather than state programmes. She waits for neighbours to prove the machines first, true to her steady style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to pray on this and look after each other, because the companies won't. I'd say government shouldn't just hand out money, they should make sure there's still honest work. I'd say it at church and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think fruit prices would drop hard, because the big orchards would run on robots with no wages to pay. We're mid-sized, we'd be squeezed from both sides. Four months of savings and a pressing shed loan is not a lot of room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut costs straight away, starting with the new pressing line we'd planned. I'd push the farm shop and the cider harder, maybe open the orchard for weddings and blossom walks, something a robot can't sell. And I'd ask Yusuf and his wife whether they could help out more for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying a lot more, put it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most about two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, and how fast it all moves. Two years doesn't give you time to watch the neighbours try it first. You'd be guessing, and I don't like guessing with the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about other ways to make money from the orchard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's where I'd go. People will still want a nice place to get married under the trees. A robot can pick an apple, but it can't make an afternoon in an orchard feel like something.

S2.say: She'd say at church and to anyone listening that people need to pray and look after each other, and the government should protect honest work rather than just hand out money.
S2.think: Privately she expects fruit prices to fall hard as big orchards go robotic, leaving her mid-sized farm squeezed with four months of savings and a pressing shed loan.
S2.do: Cancels a planned new pressing line to cut costs straight away. Pushes the farm shop and cider and opens the orchard for weddings and blossom walks, and asks her son and his wife to help out more.
S2.quote: Two years doesn't give you time to watch the neighbours try it first.
S2.fieldNote: The speed is the problem for her because it breaks her proof-first approach. She responds by leaning on what machines can't offer: experience, place and family help. Her faith frames both her public line and how she copes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to prepare properly, so let's not waste it. I'd tell the growers' group to get ready together and support each other, not wait for a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough. I'd be sixty-three, the shed loan nearly paid, and we'd have the weddings and walks going. It's still fast, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the orchard weddings in the first year, small, maybe ten a summer. I'd rent a picking robot once the neighbours had it working, probably by year two. And I'd sit down with Yusuf to agree whether he takes over the farm or the events side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I'd feel I was doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in those five years that you couldn't in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watch, learn and then buy. Two years is guessing. Five years is good sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you want your apprentices to spend those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learning pruning and machines both, and how to run events too. I'd want them able to earn a living whatever happens.

S3.say: She'd tell the growers' group that five years is time to prepare properly together and support each other rather than wait for help from outside.
S3.think: Privately five years is enough: sixty-three, the shed loan nearly paid and the events business going, still fast but with a visible path.
S3.do: Starts small orchard weddings in the first year, about ten a summer, and rents a picking robot by year two once neighbours have it working. Agrees with her son whether he takes over the farm or the events side.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steady, feeling she's doing something.
S3.quote: Watch, learn and then buy. Two years is guessing. Five years is good sense.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, her steady style works again and her mood eases. She builds a second income around place and experience. Family succession becomes an active conversation rather than an assumption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it well and keep our communities strong. Apprenticeships and family businesses should come first. I'd say it at church and at the growers' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a comfortable one for me. I'd hand over to Yusuf around sixty-five, the farm would have its robots and its weddings, and I'd still be there for blossom week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring in picking robots gradually once proven, probably by 2029. I'd grow the events side steadily and pass the business to Yusuf over five years. We'd keep saving and pay the shed loan off early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a good handover, not a loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you to sixty-eight. Where does that leave you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, I hope. The robots don't care about blossom, but people do, and I'd be there with a flask of tea watching the valley go white.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would blossom week look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopefully Yusuf's children running about in it.

S4.say: She'd say at church and the growers' group that a decade should be used well to keep communities strong, with apprenticeships and family businesses first.
S4.think: Privately it's a comfortable scenario: hand over to her son around sixty-five, with robots and weddings in place, and still be there for blossom week.
S4.do: Brings in proven picking robots gradually, probably by 2029, and grows the events side steadily. Passes the business to her son over five years and pays the shed loan off early.
S4.feel: Calm, a good handover rather than a loss.
S4.quote: The robots don't care about blossom, but people do, and I'd be there with a flask of tea watching the valley go white.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, she sees AGI as something her family business can absorb. Her identity rests on place, family and season, which machines don't threaten in her eyes. She ends looking forward to grandchildren in the orchard.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to watch and learn. What would help is the government making sure big companies can't undercut family farms with robots overnight, and funding apprenticeships so young people still learn a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: About faith, maybe. People ask what we'll do, but not what we'll believe in. I think we'll need church and community more than ever if the work goes.

headlineQuote: I think we'll need church and community more than ever if the work goes.
portrait: Zoe Farah, 58, runs an apple and pear orchard with sheep under the trees, while her husband Ibrahim runs the juice and cider press. She's warm, devout and traditional, values apprenticeships and family, and uses AI tools now and then where they've proved themselves. Unlike many farmers, she sees picking robots partly as a relief from years of hunting for pickers. She's calm in the milder scenarios and anxious if AGI arrives in two years, but with more time she builds an orchard events business and hands the farm to her son.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries her most, because there'd be no time to watch neighbours try the machines and fruit prices would fall hard.
whatWouldHelp: Rules to stop big companies undercutting family farms with robots overnight, and funded apprenticeships so young people still learn a trade.
